On NP∩coNP{\mbox{NP}\cap{\mbox{co}\mbox{NP}}} proof complexity generators

Jan KrajíčekORCID:0000-0003-0670-3957 Address: Faculty of Mathematics and Physics, Charles University, Prague Email address: jan.krajicek@protonmail.com
Abstract.

Motivated by the theory of proof complexity generators we consider the following Σ2p\Sigma^{p}_{2} search problem DDP\mbox{DD}_{P} determined by a propositional proof system PP: given a PP-proof π\pi of a disjunction ⋁iαi\bigvee_{i}\alpha_{i}, no two αi\alpha_{i} having an atom in common, find ii such that αi∈TAUT\alpha_{i}\in\mbox{TAUT}.

We formulate a hypothesis (ST) that for some strong proof system PP the problem DDP\mbox{DD}_{P} is not solvable in the student-teacher model with a p-time student and a constant number of rounds. The hypothesis follows from the existence of hard one-way permutations.

We prove, using a model-theoretic assumption, that (ST) implies NP≠c​o​NP\mbox{NP}\neq co\mbox{NP}. The assumption concerns the existence of extensions of models of a bounded arithmetic theory and it is open at present if it holds.

Key words and phrases: 
proof complexity, bounded arithmetic, student-teacher computations, search problems

Introduction

Proof complexity generators are some maps g:{0,1}∗→{0,1}∗g:{\{0,1\}^{*}}\rightarrow{\{0,1\}^{*}} with |g⁡(x)||g(x)| determined by and larger than |x||x|. Their purpose is to ”generate” hard tautologies: propositional formulas τ​(g)b\tau(g)_{b} expressing that b∉R​n​g​(g)b\notin Rng(g). To be able to express this propositionally we need that gg is p-time or more generally NP∩coNP{\mbox{NP}\cap{\mbox{co}\mbox{NP}}} (possibly non-uniform).

For NP∩coNP{\mbox{NP}\cap{\mbox{co}\mbox{NP}}} maps11 1 These are maps for which the binary predicate the ii-th bit of g⁡(x)g(x) is in NP∩coNP{\mbox{NP}\cap{\mbox{co}\mbox{NP}}}. gg sending nn bits to m>nm>n bits and b∈{0,1}mb\in{\{0,1\}^{m}}, the statement b∉R​n​g​(g)b\notin Rng(g) has the form

∀x⁡(|x|=n)​∃i<m​∀yi​Ab​(x,i,yi)\forall x(|x|=n)\exists i<m\forall y_{i}\ A_{b}(x,i,y_{i}) (1)

with AbA_{b} an open formula in the language LPV{L_{\mbox{\tiny PV}}} having a function symbol for every p-time clocked algorithm, and expressing that yiy_{i} does not witness that the ii-th bit of g⁡(x)g(x) is bib_{i}, the ii-th bit of bb.

The provability of such a statement in the true universal LPV{L_{\mbox{\tiny PV}}}-theory TPV{T_{\mbox{\tiny PV}}} can be analyzed using the interactive student-teacher model (abbr. S-T) of [15]. In this model S (the student) upon receiving x:=ax:=a proposes its first candidate solution i1i_{1}. If it is correct T (the teacher) will acknowledge this and the computation stops with i1i_{1} as its output. Otherwise she will send to S a counter-example, some w1w_{1} such that ¬Ab​(a,i1,w1)\neg A_{b}(a,i_{1},w_{1}). In that case the computation enters the second round with S proposing a second candidate solution i2i_{2} and T either accepting it or returning a counter-example w2w_{2}. The computation goes for a number of rounds until a solution is found.

We are interested in the case where the number of rounds is bounded by a constant. The S-T model makes sense for general total search problems where the condition for the acceptance of a solution, here ∀y​¬Ab​(x,i,y)\forall y\ \neg A_{b}(x,i,y), starts with a universal quantifier. Here all such search problems will be Σ2p\Sigma^{p}_{2} and following [12] we denote by

ST​[F,t​(n)]\mbox{ST}[\mbox{F},t(n)]

the class of total Σ2p\Sigma^{p}_{2} search problems such that there is a student whose moves are computed by an algorithm from F that solves the problems in t⁡(n)t(n) rounds interacting with any teacher.

There are two candidate NP∩coNP{\mbox{NP}\cap{\mbox{co}\mbox{NP}}} proof complexity generators: an NW generator and a gadget generator based on a non-deterministic circuit as the gadget, cf. [12]. An analysis using the S-T model for (1) for the NW-generator was performed in [8] and it was shown that (1) cannot be witnessed in ST​[P/p​o​l​y,O​(1)]\mbox{ST}[\mbox{P}/poly,O(1)] if a one-way permutation hard for p-size circuits exists. The gadget generator was analyzed in [12] and a similar result was shown assuming a certain plausibly looking computational hardness hypothesis (K), cf. [12, Sec.8.6].

These first-order constructions gave independence results for the theory TPV{T_{\mbox{\tiny PV}}}. There is a close relation between first-order theories and (tacitly propositional) proof systems, based on the notion of propositional translations (for theories in LPV{L_{\mbox{\tiny PV}}} this goes back to [4, 13]). It is also a classic fact that lengths-of-proofs lower bounds for formulas γ\gamma are essentially equivalent to constructing models of a suitable theory where γ\gamma can be falsified.

When trying to get from the independence results for the two NP∩coNP{\mbox{NP}\cap{\mbox{co}\mbox{NP}}} generators lengths-of-proofs lower bounds for the corresponding τ\tau-formulas one runs into the issue that the propositional translation is not entirely faithful in the following sense (this is discussed in detail as a ”missing reflection” in [8]).

The τ⁡(g)\tau(g) formulas for an NP∩coNP{\mbox{NP}\cap{\mbox{co}\mbox{NP}}}-map gg have the form

γ⁡(p,q):=⋁iβi​(p,qi)\gamma(p,q)\ :=\ \bigvee_{i}\beta_{i}(p,q^{i}) (2)

with tuples of atoms p,q=(qi)ip,q=(q^{i})_{i} and tuples qiq^{i} disjoint. A falsifying assignment to γ\gamma exists in a model iff the model satisfies

∃x,y​∀i<m​¬Ab​(x,i,(y)i)\exists x,y\forall i<m\ \neg A_{b}(x,i,(y)_{i}) (3)

where yy is a list of strings (y)i(y)_{i}, i<mi<m. The constructions in [8, 12] yield models satisfying the negation of (1)

∃x​∀i<m​∃yi​¬Ab​(x,i,yi).\exists x\forall i<m\exists y_{i}\ \neg A_{b}(x,i,y_{i})\ . (4)

To get (3) from (4) one needs the sharply bounded collection scheme BB of [3] for open LPV{L_{\mbox{\tiny PV}}}-formulas allowing to switch the two inner quantifiers. Unfortunately by [6] this principle is not provable in TPV{T_{\mbox{\tiny PV}}} (unless factoring is not hard) while adding it to TPV{T_{\mbox{\tiny PV}}} makes the proof-theoretic analysis of (1) from [8, 12] invalid (the KPT theorem of [16] does not apply in any usable form to this non-universal theory).

In this note we propose a model-theoretic method how to bypass the BB scheme and get lengths-of-proofs lower bounds from a hypothesis that a certain Σ2p\Sigma^{p}_{2} search problem is hard for S-T computations. The model-theoretic assumption is of the form saying that certain extensions of models of TPV{T_{\mbox{\tiny PV}}} exist. The caveat is that such extensions are known to exist for models satisfying the BB scheme for open formulas but it is not known in general. However, model theory seems to offer much more room to vary arguments than proof theory does and we think it is worthwhile to try to assert the model theoretic statement needed.

The paper is organized as follows. The relevant search problem and the hypothesis about its S-T intractability are discussed in Section 1, the model theoretic assumption is explained in Section 2 and the theorem reducing lengths-of-proofs lower bounds to Hypothesis (ST) is stated and proved in Section 3.

We assume that the reader is familiar with basic proof complexity theory. We do use quite a lot of notions and facts and it is unfeasible to review it here (the review would be substantially longer than the technical part). However, the reader can find all what we use in [10]. We formulate the result and the arguments without referring to proof complexity generators to make it available also to readers not familiar with that theory, although that is the primary motivation for this research. The reader can find everything that we use in [12].

A convention: letters p,q,…p,q,\dots, possibly with superscripts pi,qi,…p^{i},q^{i},\dots denote tuples of propositional atoms.

1. The search problem and its S-T computability

A propositional disjunction ⋁i<rαi\bigvee_{i<r}\alpha_{i} is a disjoint disjunction, denoted

⋁˙i<m​αi,\dot{\bigvee}_{i<m}\alpha_{i}\ ,

if no two αi\alpha_{i} have an atom in common. We often leave mm out, and write just ⋁˙i​αi\dot{\bigvee}_{i}\alpha_{i}, as mm is bounded by the size of the formula. Recall from [5] that a propositional proof system (abbr. pps) is a p-time decidable binary relation P⁡(x,y)P(x,y) such that the condition ∃x​P​(x,y)\exists xP(x,y) defines TAUT. Instead of writing P⁡(σ,β)P(\sigma,\beta) we use the suggestive notation σ:P⊢β\sigma:P\vdash\beta for the provability relation: σ\sigma is a PP-proof of β\beta. The symbol P⊢βP\vdash\beta means that β\beta has a PP-proof.

Given a pps PP, the Σ2p\Sigma^{p}_{2} search problem DDP\mbox{DD}_{P} is:

  • •

    input: a pair π,⋁˙i​αi\pi,\dot{\bigvee}_{i}\alpha_{i} s.t. π:P⊢⋁˙i​αi\pi:P\vdash\dot{\bigvee}_{i}\alpha_{i},

  • •

    solution: any ii s.t. αi∈TAUT\alpha_{i}\in\mbox{TAUT}.

The problem can be solved in the S-T model described in the Introduction. S, upon receiving an input, proposes his first candidate solution i1i_{1}. If it is correct T acknowledges it. Otherwise she sends to S a counter-example: an assignment falsifying αi1\alpha_{i_{1}}. S then proposes his second candidate solution, using also the counter-example he learned in the first round, and the computation proceeds analogously for some number of rounds.

Following [12, Def.2.4.3] we define a strong pps to be an extension of EF (Extended Frege, cf. [5]) by a p-time set of tautologies as extra axioms (see [12, Thm.2.4.4] for their nice properties). Every pps can be p-simulated by a strong one.

Hypothesis (ST): There exists a strong pps PP such that DDP∉ST​[P,O⁡(1)]\mbox{DD}_{P}\notin\mbox{ST}[\mbox{P},O(1)], P standing here also for the class of p-time algorithms computing functions.

In fact, we do think that the hypothesis is true for all strong proof systems (which is equivalent to saying that it holds for EF, the Extended Frege proof system) but for the statement this apparently weaker formulation suffices.

The DDP\mbox{DD}_{P} problem is a special case of a problem with a larger class of inputs applying to formulas of the form (2); we shall call the problem here DP\mbox{D}_{P}:

  • •

    input: a triple π,⋁iβi​(p,qi),a\pi,\bigvee_{i}\beta_{i}(p,q^{i}),a s.t. π:P⊢⋁iβi\pi:P\vdash\bigvee_{i}\beta_{i}, only atoms pp can occur in more than one βi\beta_{i}, and aa is a truth assignment to atoms pp,

  • •

    solution: any ii s.t. βi​(a,qi)∈TAUT\beta_{i}(a,q^{i})\in\mbox{TAUT}.

Lemma 1.
DDP∉ST​[P,O⁡(1)]⇔DP∉ST​[P,O⁡(1)]\mbox{DD}_{P}\notin\mbox{ST}[\mbox{P},O(1)]\Leftrightarrow\mbox{D}_{P}\notin\mbox{ST}[\mbox{P},O(1)]

The possibility that DP∈ST​[P,O⁡(1)]\mbox{D}_{P}\in\mbox{ST}[\mbox{P},O(1)] holds for strong proof systems was considered in [17]. However, it was shown in [11] that this is not true (assuming the existence of strong one-way permutations), essentially for reasons similar to why the feasible interpolation fails for them (cf. [10, Chpt.18]). The problem to witness (1) studied in [8] does not have a PP-proof as a part of the input and this led to the need to consider non-uniform p-time students there. Another plausibly looking hypothesis about the feasible intractability of a certain search problem related to non-deterministic circuits and implying (ST) was given in [12] (cf. hypothesis (K) there).

We state for the record the plausibility of (ST).

Lemma 2 ([11]).

(ST) is true if a strong one-way permutation exists (no polynomial size circuit can invert it with a non-negligible advantage).

2. Bounded arithmetic models

The classic theorem we shall recall now uses the correspondence between first-order theories and proof systems mentioned in the Introduction. A prototype of the statement was proved in [14, Thm.1] working with theory S21S^{1}_{2} of [3] and its relation to Extended Frege proof system EF (a consequence of [4]). The same argument applies to any pair of corresponding theories and proof systems using the generalization of [4] developed in [13]. The underlying argument is discussed in detail also in [10, Sec.20.1].

As we are aiming at all proof systems at once we can work with the theory TPV{T_{\mbox{\tiny PV}}} and avoid discussing the correspondence between theories and proof systems. The first item of the theorem speaks about propositional proof systems and by those we mean proof systems determined by standard p-time binary relations and not proof systems in the sense of the non-standard model. In particular, a pps PP may be incomplete in a model of TPV{T_{\mbox{\tiny PV}}} but it will always be sound as that is expressible by a universal LPV{L_{\mbox{\tiny PV}}}-formula.

Theorem 3 (after [14, Thm.1]).

Assume 𝐌\mathbf{M} is a non-standard model of TPV{T_{\mbox{\tiny PV}}} and let φ∈𝐌\varphi\in{\mathbf{M}} be a propositional formula (in the sense of the model). The following two statements are equivalent:

  1. (1)

    φ\varphi has no proof in 𝐌\mathbf{M} in any proof system.

  2. (2)

    There exists an extension 𝐌′⊇𝐌{\mathbf{M}}^{\prime}\supseteq{\mathbf{M}} such that

    𝐌′⊧TPV+(¬φ)∈SAT.{\mathbf{M}}^{\prime}\ \models\ {T_{\mbox{\tiny PV}}}\ +\ (\neg\varphi)\in\mbox{SAT}\ .

The fact that the construction in [14] works with models of S21S^{1}_{2} implies that 𝐌′{\mathbf{M}}^{\prime} preserves (i.e. will satisfy) all Σ1b\Sigma^{b}_{1} properties of elements of 𝐌\mathbf{M} true there (this uses that the models satisfy the sharply bounded collection principle BB for open Σ1b\Sigma^{b}_{1}-formulas, a consequence of S21S^{1}_{2} (cf. [3, 7]).

Further it is remarked at the end of [14] that one can arrange that 𝐌′{\mathbf{M}}^{\prime} introduces no new lengths into 𝐌{\mathbf{M}}:

L​o​g​(𝐌′)=L​o​g​(𝐌)Log({\mathbf{M}}^{\prime})=Log({\mathbf{M}}) (5)

where L​o​g​(𝐌)={|m||m∈𝐌}Log({\mathbf{M}})\ =\ \{|m|\ |\ m\in{\mathbf{M}}\}. A construction which yields this (with an additional requirement on 𝐌\mathbf{M}) is the forcing construction underlying [7, Thm.9.4.2].

The problem we are interested in is whether these two properties, that is item 2 of Theorem 3 and (5), can be arranged too if we only know that 𝐌⊧TPV{\mathbf{M}}\models{T_{\mbox{\tiny PV}}}. We shall formulate the problem in a less direct way but closer to the construction in the proof of [7, Thm.9.4.2]. This formulation also relates better to the possibility to use Boolean-valued models discussed at the end of [9].

Problem 2.1.

Assume 𝐌⊧TPV\mathbf{M}\models{T_{\mbox{\tiny PV}}} and that it satisfies Condition 1 in Theorem 3. Does it follow that there are LPV{L_{\mbox{\tiny PV}}}-structures 𝐌∗,𝐌′{\mathbf{M}}^{*},{\mathbf{M}}^{\prime}:

𝐌⊆𝐌∗⊆𝐌′{\mathbf{M}}\subseteq{\mathbf{M}}^{*}\subseteq{\mathbf{M}}^{\prime}

such that

  1. (1)

    𝐌∗{\mathbf{M}}^{*} preserves all Σ1b​(P​V)\Sigma^{b}_{1}(PV)-properties of elements of 𝐌{\mathbf{M}},

  2. (2)

    𝐌′⊧TPV+(¬φ)∈SAT{\mathbf{M}}^{\prime}\models{T_{\mbox{\tiny PV}}}+(\neg\varphi)\in\mbox{SAT},

  3. (3)

    L​o​g​(𝐌∗)=L​o​g​(𝐌′)Log({\mathbf{M}}^{*})=Log({\mathbf{M}}^{\prime})?

The assumption we shall use in Theorem 4 is that the problem has the affirmative solution. Note that the negative answer implies P≠NP\mbox{P}\neq\mbox{NP} as otherwise22 2 If ff is a p-time algorithm that finds a satisfying assignment for all satisfiable formulas then this fact, being a universal statement, would be in TPV{T_{\mbox{\tiny PV}}} and hence TPV{T_{\mbox{\tiny PV}}} would prove all true bounded formulas. TPV{T_{\mbox{\tiny PV}}} proves S21​(PV){S^{1}_{2}(\mbox{PV}}).

The problem asks about all models of TPV{T_{\mbox{\tiny PV}}} but it would suffice to get the affirmative answer for a sufficiently universal class of models (e.g. countable or recursively saturated). Also, it suffices if 𝐌∗{\mathbf{M}}^{*} preserves from 𝐌\mathbf{M} properties of the form ∀i​∃y​B​(x,i,y)\forall i\exists yB(x,i,y) with ii sharply bounded, yy bounded and BB open.

Let us remark that constructing extensions of bounded arithmetic models introducing no new lengths is very close to constructing expansions of non-standard finite structures. Such expansions are at the heart of applications of model theory to lower bounds for circuits or proofs as it is spectacularly demonstrated in [1, 2]. Developing such constructions is in my view a crucial task in proof complexity; the survey [9] discusses this in detail (cf. also [10, Chpt.20])).

3. The theorem

Universal LPV{L_{\mbox{\tiny PV}}} sentences ∀x​A​(x)\forall xA(x) can be translated into a sequence of p-size propositional formulas ‖A‖n|\mkern-2.5mu|A|\mkern-2.5mu|^{n} such that

∀x⁡(|x|=n)​A​(x)↔‖A‖n∈TAUT\forall x(|x|=n)A(x)\leftrightarrow|\mkern-2.5mu|A|\mkern-2.5mu|^{n}\in\mbox{TAUT}\

(cf. [7] or [10, Sec.12.6]).

For a pps PP let R​e​fPRef_{P} be the universal valid LPV{L_{\mbox{\tiny PV}}} formula

x:P⊢y→(¬y)∉SATx:P\vdash y\ \rightarrow(\neg y)\notin\mbox{SAT}

where we simplify the notation and write ¬y\neg y for the p-time function sending a code of a formula to the code of its negation.

Theorem 4.

Assume that Problem 2.1 has the affirmative solution. Then Hypothesis (ST) implies NP≠c​o​NP\mbox{NP}\neq co\mbox{NP}.

Proof :

(1)

Assume for the sake of a contradiction that the hypothesis (ST) and NP=coNP\mbox{NP}={\mbox{co}\mbox{NP}} both hold. We shall bring it to a contradiction using the model-theoretic assumption. Take a strong pps PP that satisfies the condition in (ST) and is also p-bounded.

(2)

Consider theory SS in the language extending LPV{L_{\mbox{\tiny PV}}} by two constant symbols: π\pi and α\alpha, and having the following axioms:

  • •

    TPV{T_{\mbox{\tiny PV}}},

  • •

    α\alpha is a disjoint disjunction of the form ⋁˙i<m​αi\dot{\bigvee}_{i<m}\alpha_{i} (mm is determined by α\alpha),

  • •

    π:P⊢α\pi:P\vdash\alpha,

  • •

    ∀i<m⁡(¬αi)∈SAT\forall i<m\ (\neg\alpha_{i})\in\mbox{SAT}.

If SS were inconsistent then applying the KPT theorem (cf. [16, 7, 12]) to the universal theory with axioms listed in the first three items would give p-time functions computing moves of a student that solves DDP\mbox{DD}_{P} in a constant number of rounds, thus violating (ST).

Let 𝐌\mathbf{M} be a model (necessarily non-standard) of SS.

(3)

Assume c≥1c\geq 1 is a constant such that any β∈TAUT\beta\in\mbox{TAUT} has a PP-proof of size ≤|β|c\leq|\beta|^{c}. We shall abbreviate by

σ:P⊢∗β\sigma:P\vdash_{*}\beta

the formula

(σ:P⊢β)∧(|σ|≤|β|c).(\sigma:P\vdash\beta)\ \wedge\ (|\sigma|\leq|\beta|^{c})\ .

In the following formula the symbols (y)i(y)_{i} and (z)i(z)_{i} denote the ii-th string in the list coded by y,zy,z, respectively, and l​e​n​(y)≤|y|len(y)\leq|y| denotes the number of these strings.

Claim: For any pps QQ the universal formula AQA_{Q}:

x:P⊢⋁˙i(y)i→Q⊬||∀i<len(y)(z)i:P⊬∗(y)i||x:P\vdash\dot{\bigvee}_{i}(y)_{i}\ \rightarrow\ Q\not\vdash|\mkern-2.5mu|\forall i<len(y)\ (z)_{i}:P\not\vdash_{*}(y)_{i}|\mkern-2.5mu| (6)

(we leave the obvious length-bounds in the translation out) is true and hence in TPV{T_{\mbox{\tiny PV}}}.

The claim holds because some (y)i(y)_{i} has to be a tautology and hence - by the p-boundedness of PP - would have a short PP-proof.

(4)

All AQA_{Q} hold in 𝐌\mathbf{M} and we can substitute x:=πx:=\pi and y:=αy:=\alpha. This yields

𝐌⊧Q⊬φ⁡(r){\mathbf{M}}\ \models\ Q\not\vdash\varphi(r)

where φ⁡(r)\varphi(r) is obtained from

||∀i<len(y)(z)i:P⊬∗(y)i||(r,q)|\mkern-2.5mu|\forall i<len(y)\ (z)_{i}:P\not\vdash_{*}(y)_{i}|\mkern-2.5mu|(r,q)

by substituting the bits of α\alpha for atoms qq (hence the sharply bounded universal quantifier becomes ⋀i<m\bigwedge_{i<m}) and the remaining atoms rr correspond to (bits of) zz.

(5)

Now we conclude the proof by using the assumption that Problem 2.1 has the affirmative solution. This gives us 𝐌⊆𝐌∗⊆𝐌′{\mathbf{M}}\subseteq{\mathbf{M}}^{*}\subseteq{\mathbf{M}}^{\prime} such that

L​o​g​(𝐌∗)=L​o​g​(𝐌′),Log({\mathbf{M}}^{*})=Log({\mathbf{M}}^{\prime})\ , (7)

and 𝐌′⊧TPV∧¬φ∈SAT{\mathbf{M}}^{\prime}\models{T_{\mbox{\tiny PV}}}\wedge\neg\varphi\in\mbox{SAT}. Note that 𝐌∗{\mathbf{M}}^{*} satisfies the last axiom of SS:

𝐌∗⊧∀i<m⁡(¬αi)∈SAT{\mathbf{M}}^{*}\ \models\ \forall i<m\ (\neg\alpha_{i})\in\mbox{SAT}\ (8)

as it preserves the Σ1b​(P​V)\Sigma^{b}_{1}(PV)-properties from 𝐌\mathbf{M}.

Let σ∈𝐌′\sigma\in{\mathbf{M}}^{\prime} be an assignment to the atoms rr that falsifies the formula φ\varphi in 𝐌′{\mathbf{M}}^{\prime}. Hence σ=(σi)i<m\sigma=(\sigma_{i})_{i<m} and we have

𝐌′⊧σi0:P⊢αi0{\mathbf{M}}^{\prime}\ \models\ \sigma_{i_{0}}:P\vdash\alpha_{i_{0}}

for some i0<mi_{0}<m. But by (7) ioi_{o} is also already in 𝐌∗{\mathbf{M}}^{*} and hence by (8) we get:

𝐌′⊧(¬αi0)∈SAT.{\mathbf{M}}^{\prime}\ \models\ (\neg\alpha_{i_{0}})\in\mbox{SAT}\ .

That contradicts R​e​fPRef_{P} which holds in 𝐌′{\mathbf{M}}^{\prime} as it models TPV{T_{\mbox{\tiny PV}}}.

∎

Note that the proof yields a somewhat stronger conclusion that in no strong PP can a proof of some disjunct in a disjoint disjunction be polynomially bounded in size in terms of a proof of the disjunction (i.e. the strong feasible disjunction property fails for strong proof systems, cf.[12])

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

  • Click the "Report Issue" () button, located in the page header.

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Our team has already identified the following issues. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for all.

Have a free development cycle? Help support accessibility at arXiv! Our collaborators at LaTeXML maintain a list of packages that need conversion, and welcome developer contributions.
